AdamW.d: Adam with weight decay: every number’s step is divided by a running average of its own past gradients’ size, so each number moves about the same amount.

BLEU.d: A score from 0 to 100 for how many of the answer’s word runs also appear in the reference answer.

BPE.d: Byte-pair encoding: a tokenizer that builds its tokens by gluing together, again and again, the pair of neighbouring pieces seen most often.

EMA.d: Exponential moving average: a copy of the weights that follows training slowly, smoothing its jitter.

FlashAttention.d: A way of computing attention a block at a time that never holds the whole table of scores — the same result, far less memory. It is built into PyTorch: F.scaled_dot_product_attention uses it by itself, only on a recent NVIDIA GPU, in fp16 or bf16, with no mask tensor (deep dive 20). This notebook does not implement it.

KV cache.d: The keys and values of the tokens already written, kept so each new step only works on the newest token.

Muon.d: An optimizer that turns each weight matrix’s update into one that moves every direction by the same amount.

Newton–Schulz.d: A few matrix products that bring every singular value of a matrix close to 1 without turning any of its directions.

QK-Norm.d: Bringing every head’s query and key to the same size before they are compared, so a score cannot grow just because the vectors grew.

RMSNorm.d: A normalisation that divides a vector by its root mean square (its typical size) and scales it.

RoPE.d: Rotary position embedding: pairs of numbers are turned by an angle that grows with the token’s position.

SwiGLU.d: A feed-forward with a gate: one copy of the input decides, unit by unit, how much of the other passes.

argmax.d: The position of the largest value: logits.argmax(0) gives, for every pixel, the class with the larger score.
argmax.a: Pointing at the tallest person in the room.

attention.d: Each word gathering information from other words, with shares (weights) that add up to 100%.

autograd.d: PyTorch records every operation on tensors that need gradients; loss.backward() walks that record backwards and fills each parameter’s .grad with how the loss changes as it changes.
autograd.a: A trail of breadcrumbs that lets the blame for a mistake be traced back to every dial.

batch.d: The examples worked on together in one training step.

beam search.d: Keeping several candidate answers at once, extending each, and returning the best-scoring one.

broadcasting.d: When two tensors of different shapes are combined, axes of size 1 are stretched to match: a (3, 1, 1) mean subtracts from every pixel of a (3, H, W) picture.
broadcasting.a: One instruction read out to the whole class instead of to each pupil.

causal.d: The decoder writes left to right, so while training each position may only look at itself and the positions before it — otherwise it could copy the answer it is meant to predict.
causal.a: Covering the rest of the page while you read a line.

checkpoint.d: The parameters saved to a file at some point in training.

class.d: class Name: defines a new kind of object: the data it keeps (attributes, self.x) and the functions that work on it (methods). Name(...) makes one, an instance.
class.a: A blueprint; every house built from it is an instance.

classmethod.d: A method that receives the class itself (cls) instead of an object — the usual way to write another way to make an object, like BPETokenizer.load(path).
classmethod.a: A second door into the factory: it still makes the same product.

collate.d: How a DataLoader turns a list of items into one batch. Sentences have different lengths, so here each batch is padded to its own longest sentence.
collate.a: Lining up children of different heights for a photo by giving the shorter ones a step.

comprehension.d: A loop written inside brackets that builds a list, dict or set in one expression: [f(x) for x in xs]. Same result as a for loop that appends, in one line.
comprehension.a: Telling a helper “one of these for each of those” instead of handing items over one by one.

constant.d: Python has no real constants; a name in CAPITALS tells the reader “set once here, read everywhere, never changed while running”. Changing it here changes the whole run.
constant.a: The numbers written on the recipe card before you start cooking.

context-manager.d: An object used with with: it does something on entry and is guaranteed to undo it on exit, even if an error happens. @contextmanager makes one from a generator: the code before yield runs on entry, after it on exit.
context-manager.a: Borrowing a tool with a sign-out sheet: it always gets returned.

cosine decay.d: Lowering the learning rate along half a cosine curve: slowly at first, faster in the middle, gently at the end.
cosine decay.a: Easing off the accelerator smoothly as you approach the destination.

counter.d: Counter is a dict that counts: a missing key reads as 0, so c[x] += 1 just works. defaultdict(set) gives a new empty set for a missing key.
counter.a: A tally sheet with a line ready for every word, even ones not seen yet.

cross-entropy.d: For each pixel: minus the log of the probability the model gave the right class, averaged. 0 when it is certain and right; large when it is sure and wrong.
cross-entropy.a: A fine that grows the more confidently you bet on the wrong horse.

dataloader.d: PyTorch’s way of handing a training loop its batches. With batch_size=None it passes on whatever the dataset yields, already batched.
dataloader.a: The conveyor belt to the oven.

decoder.d: The half of the model that writes the answer, one token at a time.

decorator.d: @something on the line above a def hands the function to something, which wraps it. @torch.no_grad() runs the whole method without recording gradients.
decorator.a: A sticker on a folder that tells the office how to handle it.

device.d: Where a tensor’s numbers live and are computed: cpu, cuda (an NVIDIA GPU) or mps (an Apple-silicon GPU). Two tensors must be on the same device to be combined; .to(device) moves one.
device.a: Which kitchen the cooking happens in: ingredients have to be in the same kitchen to be mixed.

dict.d: A dictionary: values found by a key, d["key"]. dict(a=1) is the same as {"a": 1}.

dropout.d: While training, sets a random share of the numbers to 0 (and scales the rest up), so the model cannot lean on any one of them. Switched off by model.eval().
dropout.a: Practising with a random team-mate sitting out each round, so nobody becomes indispensable.

dtype.d: The kind of number a tensor holds: float32 for most model numbers, int64 (“long”) for labels and counts, uint8 for image bytes.
dtype.a: Whether a column holds prices, counts or yes/no.

early-stopping.d: Stop training when the validation loss has not improved for PATIENCE epochs, and keep the best checkpoint rather than the last.
early-stopping.a: Leaving the oven once the cake stops rising, before it burns.

embedding.d: The table that turns each token id into its vector. Its numbers are learned.

encoder.d: The half of the model that reads the input sentence.

epoch.d: One pass over all the training examples.

exact match.d: 1 if the answer is exactly the reference, 0 otherwise — no partial credit.

expert.d: One of the small feed-forwards of a mixture of experts.

f-string.d: A string with f in front: anything inside {…} is worked out and written in. {x:,} adds thousands separators, {x:.1%} shows a share as a percentage.
f-string.a: A form letter whose blanks fill themselves in.

feed-forward.d: The “think” move: each word’s vector goes through a small network on its own.

flatten.d: Joins several axes into one: x.flatten(2) turns a grid (B, C, H, W) into a list (B, C, H × W).
flatten.a: Reading a page of rows as one long line.

from-import.d: Takes only some names out of a module, so the code can write DataLoader instead of torch.utils.data.DataLoader.
from-import.a: Taking two tools out of the box instead of the box.

grad-clip.d: If all gradients together form a vector longer than a limit, shrink them to that length. It stops one unlucky batch from throwing the weights far off.
grad-clip.a: A speed limiter: you can still steer anywhere, just not lurch.

greedy.d: Always writing the single most likely token.

grouped-query attention.d: Attention in which several query heads share one key/value head, so the KV cache holds fewer numbers.

head.d: One of several attentions running side by side in a layer; here 4 heads of 128 numbers each.

heap.d: A list kept in an order where the smallest item is always first: heappush adds in about log n steps, heappop takes the smallest. Storing −count makes the largest count come out first.
heap.a: A queue at a hospital: whoever is most urgent is seen next, however late they arrived.

heatmap.d: A table drawn as coloured squares: each cell’s colour shows its value. sns.heatmap draws one from a matrix, with labels along both edges.
heatmap.a: A weather map where colour stands for temperature.

id.d: A token’s number in the vocabulary. From the tokenizer on, the model sees only these numbers.

import.d: Loads a module — a file of ready-made code — and gives it a name in this notebook. import torch.nn as nn loads torch.nn and lets the code call it nn.
import.a: Taking a toolbox off the shelf and putting it on the bench, with a label on the lid.

init.d: The method Python runs when an object is made: it sets the object up. Name(a, b) calls __init__(self, a, b).
init.a: Unpacking and setting up a new appliance before first use.

int8.d: An 8-bit whole number, from −128 to 127: a quarter of the 32 bits of a float.

integer-division.d: Divides and drops the remainder: 7 // 2 is 3. Used where a count has to be a whole number.
integer-division.a: Cutting a rope into full-length pieces and leaving the scrap.

json.d: A plain-text format for data — dicts, lists, strings, numbers — that any language can read. json.load turns a file into Python objects, json.dump writes them back.
json.a: A form that every office knows how to fill in.

key.d: What a word advertises about itself, to be matched against queries.

label-smoothing.d: The target is not “100% the right token” but 90% it and the rest spread over all tokens. The model is never pushed to be infinitely sure.
label-smoothing.a: Grading “almost certainly right” as full marks, so nobody learns to shout.

lambda.d: A small function written in one expression, without a name: lambda x: x * 2.
lambda.a: A sticky note with one instruction, instead of a page in the manual.

layer.d: One round of the model’s moves — look around, then think. Layers are stacked.

linear.d: A learned matrix and a bias: every output number is a weighted sum of all the inputs, plus a constant. nn.Linear(a, b) has a × b weights and b biases.
linear.a: A mixing desk: every output channel is its own mix of all the input channels.

logit.d: A token’s raw score before softmax: higher means more likely.

lr-schedule.d: The learning rate changes over training: here it climbs from almost 0 (warmup), then falls along a cosine curve to 0, so early steps are gentle and the end settles.
lr-schedule.a: Pulling away slowly, cruising, then braking smoothly into the parking space.

map-dataset.d: A PyTorch dataset you index: __len__ says how many items there are, __getitem__(i) returns item i. The DataLoader picks indices, fetches the items and groups them into batches.
map-dataset.a: A numbered shelf: ask for number 7, get the box on shelf 7.

masks.d: A table of True / False saying which tokens each token may look at. Padding is hidden from everyone; in the decoder, every token is also hidden from the tokens before it.
masks.a: Blinkers: some of the room is simply out of view.

matmul.d: Every row of the left matrix against every column of the right one: each pair gives one number, a sum of products. Q @ K.T gives every query against every key.
matmul.a: Comparing every applicant with every job description and writing down a score for each pair.

matplotlib.d: Python’s plotting library: plt.subplots makes a grid of panels, imshow draws a picture or a grid of numbers in one of them.

memo-cache.d: Remembering a function’s answer for an input, so the second time the same input comes the answer is looked up instead of computed.
memo-cache.a: Writing a sum’s answer in the margin so you never redo it.

mixed-precision.d: Running most arithmetic in 16-bit numbers (bfloat16 or float16) on a GPU — about twice as fast — while keeping sensitive parts in 32 bits. float16 needs a GradScaler so small gradients do not round to zero.
mixed-precision.a: Doing rough sums on a notepad and the final accounts in the ledger.

mixture of experts.d: Several small feed-forwards (experts) and a router that sends each token to a few of them.

momentum.d: A running average of past gradients, so that one noisy batch cannot swing the step much.

multi-token prediction.d: Training an extra head to guess the token after next, not only the next one.

nn-module.d: The base of every PyTorch model part. A class that inherits from it gets its parameters tracked automatically, can be moved with .to(), switched between train() and eval(), saved with state_dict(), and is called like a function: layer(x) runs forward(x).
nn-module.a: A standard socket: anything built to it plugs into everything else.

no-grad.d: Inside it, PyTorch does not record operations for gradients: less memory and faster, for code that only uses the model.
no-grad.a: Doing a calculation in pen without keeping the working.

nonlocal.d: Inside an inner function, nonlocal x means: assigning x changes the enclosing function’s variable, not a new local one.
nonlocal.a: Writing on the shared whiteboard rather than on your own notepad.

normalisation.d: Rescaling a vector to a steady size, so no layer is flooded by big numbers or starved by tiny ones.

online softmax.d: Softmax computed piece by piece, keeping a running largest score and a running sum, rescaled whenever a larger score turns up.

optimizer.d: The part of training that turns the gradients into changes of the weights — AdamW, Muon.

orthogonalize.d: A matrix’s update with every singular value set to about 1: it moves the weights the same amount in every direction it moves them at all, instead of mostly along one or two.
orthogonalize.a: Spreading the effort evenly over every muscle instead of letting one do all the work.

overfitting.d: Learning the training examples by heart instead of the pattern behind them.

padding.d: Filler tokens (<PAD>) that make short sentences as long as the longest one in a batch.

parameter.d: One number the model learns. This model has 22,979,823 of them.

parameter-tensor.d: A tensor marked as something the model learns: it shows up in model.parameters(), the optimizer updates it, and it is saved with the model.
parameter-tensor.a: A dial on the machine, as opposed to a reading on its display.

position.d: Where a token sits in its sentence: 0, 1, 2, …

property.d: A method read like an attribute: tokenizer.vocab_size runs the method and returns its value, always up to date.
property.a: A display showing a live reading rather than a number written down once.

quantization.d: Storing numbers with fewer bits: here each weight as one of 255 whole numbers times a scale per row.

query.d: What a word is looking for. It is compared with every other word’s key.

register-buffer.d: A tensor that belongs to the module — it moves with .to(device) — but is not learned. persistent=False keeps it out of the saved state_dict, since it can be recomputed.
register-buffer.a: A reference table bolted to the machine: it travels with it but is never adjusted.

repetition penalty.d: Pushing down the score of tokens already written, so the model repeats itself less.

residual.d: x = x + layer(x): each layer adds its result to what was there instead of replacing it, so information and gradients can always flow straight through.
residual.a: Annotating a document in the margin instead of rewriting it.

router.d: A tiny layer that scores the experts for each token and picks the best few.

sampling.d: Drawing the next token at random, in proportion to its probability.

sdpa.d: F.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V) computes softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d)·V in one fused call; PyTorch can pick a fast kernel (FlashAttention) for it — never building the full score table in memory.
sdpa.a: Ordering the whole meal as a set menu instead of dish by dish: the kitchen can do it faster.

seed.d: torch.manual_seed(n) fixes the starting point of PyTorch’s random numbers, so every run makes the same “random” choices: the same weights, the same pictures, the same results.
seed.a: Shuffling a deck in exactly the same way every time, so the game can be replayed.

shape.d: How many numbers a tensor has along each axis, e.g. (batch, channels, height, width). Most mistakes in model code are shape mistakes, so the notes give the shape of every tensor.
shape.a: The dimensions of a box: how many rows, how many columns, how many layers.

singular value.d: How strongly a matrix stretches along one of its main directions.

slicing.d: x[a:b] takes positions a up to (not including) b; x[:, a:] does it on the second axis of an array; a missing end means “to the end”. x[None] adds a new axis of size 1 in front.
slicing.a: Cutting a slice from a loaf without touching the rest.

soft cap.d: cap × tanh(score / cap): small scores pass almost unchanged, none can go past the cap.

softmax.d: Turns any list of scores into shares that are all positive and add up to 1: bigger scores get bigger shares, and the gaps between scores decide how much bigger.
softmax.a: Splitting a prize in proportion to how each contestant scored — exaggerated in favour of the best.

speculative decoding.d: Writing faster by checking a cheap guess of the next token in the same pass as the token before it; a right guess gives two tokens per pass.

state-dict.d: A dict of every learned tensor of a model, by name. Saved with torch.save, loaded with load_state_dict, it rebuilds the trained model exactly.

staticmethod.d: A function kept inside a class that does not need self: called as Class.f(…) or self.f(…), it only uses its arguments.
staticmethod.a: A tool hanging in the workshop that works the same whoever picks it up.

string-block.d: """…""" is a string that may run over many lines; here it holds the whole word list, one word per line.
string-block.a: A long scroll pasted into the code.

super-init.d: Runs the parent class’s setup (here nn.Module’s) before the class adds its own parts — without it PyTorch cannot track the parameters.
super-init.a: Laying the foundation before building the walls.

temperature.d: A knob applied before drawing: below 1 it sharpens the probabilities, above 1 it flattens them.

tensor.d: PyTorch’s array: a grid of numbers with any number of axes, which can live on the GPU and remember how it was computed so gradients can flow back through it.
tensor.a: A spreadsheet that can have more than two dimensions and can do its sums on the graphics card.

token.d: A piece of a word that the model reads or writes. “sofa” is two tokens here: “sof” and “a_”.

tokenizer.d: The part that cuts text into tokens and glues tokens back into text.

top-k.d: Sampling only among the k most likely tokens.

top-p.d: Sampling only among the most likely tokens that together reach probability p.

train-eval.d: model.train() switches dropout on; model.eval() switches it off so the same input always gives the same output. They change behaviour, not weights.

training.d: Showing the model examples with their answers and nudging its parameters after each.

transpose.d: Swaps two axes: x.transpose(1, 2) turns (B, heads, patches, d) into (B, patches, heads, d). The numbers stay; how they are read changes.
transpose.a: Turning a table on its side.

try-except.d: try: runs a block; finally: runs afterwards whatever happened — error or not. Used here to make sure the trained weights always come back.
try-except.a: A safety net that is always taken down after the act, whether it was needed or not.

validation.d: Checking the model on examples kept aside, to see if it learned the pattern rather than the examples.

value.d: What a word hands over when a query matches its key.

vector.d: A list of numbers. Every token becomes a vector of 512 numbers.

view.d: Reads the same numbers with a different shape — no copying. view(-1, 1, 1) makes a list of three into a (3, 1, 1) tensor; -1 means “whatever size makes it fit”.
view.a: Rearranging the same eggs from a 2 × 6 box into a 3 × 4 box.

vocabulary.d: The full list of tokens the model knows — 16,111 in this notebook.

warmup.d: The first steps of training, during which the learning rate climbs from almost 0 to its full value, so the random starting weights are not thrown about by large steps.
warmup.a: Pulling away gently before putting your foot down.

weight decay.d: Pulling weights a little toward 0 at every step, to keep them from growing needlessly large.

with.d: Runs a block inside a context that is set up first and always undone afterwards — with torch.no_grad(): switches gradient tracking off for the block, then back on.
with.a: Borrowing a key that is handed back the moment you leave the room.

xavier.d: Starting weights drawn uniformly in a range set by the matrix’s size, so signals keep about the same size as they pass through the layers at the start of training.
xavier.a: Setting every amplifier in a chain so that no stage starts out too loud or too quiet.

zero-grad.d: Clears the gradients left by the last step. PyTorch adds new gradients to old ones, so without this every step would push with all the previous steps’ gradients too.
zero-grad.a: Wiping the whiteboard before the next sum.

zipf.d: In real text a word’s frequency is roughly 1 / its rank: the second most common word appears about half as often as the first, the tenth a tenth as often.
zipf.a: A few stars get most of the fan mail; the long tail gets a letter each.
